source.title: How Well do Feature Visualizations Support Causal Understanding of CNN Activations?
source.authors: R. Zimmermann; Judy Borowski; Robert Geirhos; M. Bethge; Thomas S. A. Wallis; Wieland Brendel

record.tranche_reason: The study uses a human psychophysical task, rather than an automated scoring method, to test whether reference visualizations help people predict the effects of interventions on CNN activations.
record.gate_note: The study measures human accuracy when predicting which of two occluded images elicits a stronger unit activation, using highly activating reference images. It does not measure neuron job counts, the fidelity of an explanation's own firing predictions, attribution graphs, or automated explanation scores. The alternative-baseline results are recorded as related findings, not as direct tests of V6.
record.test_reason: Humans shown a unit's most activating images (natural or synthetic) must predict which occlusion keeps the unit's activation higher. This is a human psychophysics test of whether understanding gained from activating examples predicts the unit's firing under intervention, so it bears on V6 in InceptionV1. It does not estimate neuron-job shares, test attribution graphs or score explanations automatically.
record.authors_conclusion: Largely correct. Feature visualizations help modestly over no references (67–68±4% vs 60±3%) but give no advantage over simpler alternatives such as dataset samples (66–67%). Simple heuristics reach the same regime, and performance depends on unit, image set and activation difference.
record.recipe_differences: The study uses human judgments of occlusion effects in an InceptionV1 image task; it does not use the neuron-pole auditing or explanation-scoring methods named in the claim versions.
record.method_sensitivity: Performance varies with unit, image set, and relative activation difference; the activation-difference trend is stronger in the P OOL branch than in the 3 × 3 branch.

fits_no_version.finding: Simple image heuristics reach 61–63% on the occlusion task, the same range as reference-supported participants. Saliency is at chance (0.49).
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: In occlusion-prediction tasks, simple image heuristics match the predictive benefit of unit visualizations.

record.problems: The main task samples only a small set of InceptionV1 units and uses fixed-size square occlusions; the authors note that these interventions limit precision and suggest testing more units and other networks. Human accuracy is not a direct measure of an explanation's own predictive fidelity.
record.rows_left_out: No other main-task outcomes were omitted. The study also reports reaction times, decision agreement, and correlations with activation differences; these do not directly measure V6's explanation-prediction claim. The appendix replication of a different forward-simulation task is not included as a V6 result.

untested.parts: All: no shares of neuron poles by number of jobs.
All: one CNN only, no language models, no scaling.
All: no test of the cat-and-car neuron, pose features or superposition.
All: no comparison of architectures, regularization or tools against interpretable shares.
All: no attribution graphs or replacement models.
Written explanations of neurons, firing on held-out inputs beyond occlusions of top images, language-model neurons, and whether 'one main job' shares are overstated.

missing.what: Per-unit accuracy. Most units are near or just above chance, one unit (layer 2 POOL) is below chance and a few, e.g. layer 8 POOL, are high. This shows unit dependence of how well activating examples predict firing.
Expert performance (two first authors) is only 1–6% above MTurk participants, giving a human upper bound on the task.
Accuracy rises with relative activation difference (Spearman up to ~0.49 in the POOL branch, weak in the 3×3 branch).
MTurk replication of the forward-simulation task: natural references 84±3% vs synthetic 65±3%.

record.verdict_notes: V6 is about written neuron explanations predicting firing; this study measures human predictive understanding from activating examples in a vision CNN. The link is close but indirect, so the support is limited to that setting. Neither original source is this study.

versions.untested_parts: The study does not estimate the shares of neuron poles with one job, two related jobs, or jobs not yet understood.
It tests neither shares across models or scales nor dense versus mixture-of-experts models.
It does not test the InceptionV1 cat-and-car example, pose detection, recursive generalization, or superposition.
It does not compare architectures, regularization, tool quality, or estimates of interpretable-neuron shares.
It does not evaluate attribution graphs or compare them with a trained replacement model.

The study tests human prediction of activation changes using reference images and occlusion interventions, not whether a neuron's own explanation accurately predicts its firing on held-out inputs or how many neuron jobs are explained.
It does not score explanations by simulating activations on new text or report automated explanation-score distributions.

rows.subject: MTurk participants
rows.size_stated: 323 crowdsourced participants across the experiment; 50 participants per reference-image condition before exclusions
rows.operation_detail: Choose which of two occluded query images activates a CNN unit more strongly, given synthetic feature-visualization references.
rows.uncertainty: ±4%; figure error bars are described as two standard errors
rows.note: The authors describe performance as only slightly higher than without references and not significantly higher than the other visualization conditions.
rows.check: Re-graded against V6. The version predicts that activating-example understanding fails to predict firing. Synthetic references give 67±4% vs 60±3% with no references, close to the 63% heuristic baselines, so the predicted failure appears nearly in full. The abstract reports 68±4%; the text reports 67±4%.

rows.subject: MTurk participants
rows.size_stated: 323 crowdsourced participants across the experiment; 50 participants per reference-image condition before exclusions
rows.operation_detail: Choose which of two occluded query images activates a CNN unit more strongly, with no reference images.
rows.uncertainty: ±3%; figure error bars are described as two standard errors
rows.note: The no-reference condition is above chance; the study reports it differs from all other conditions.
rows.check: No-reference control. It is a baseline, not an explanation from activating examples, so it cannot show V6's effect alone.

source_check.locator_found: Sec 4.1, Fig 3A (60±3%, only None differs from all others, p<0.05)

rows.subject: MTurk participants
rows.size_stated: 323 crowdsourced participants across the experiment; 50 participants per reference-image condition before exclusions
rows.operation_detail: Choose which of two occluded query images activates a CNN unit more strongly, given alternative reference visualizations.

conditions.value: Natural, Mixed, and Blur conditions; reported together as a range

rows.uncertainty: The reported range includes the stated ± values; exact value-to-condition mapping is not stated
rows.note: The text gives a range across the other visualization types but does not assign each value to Natural, Mixed, or Blur.
rows.check: Natural references are a unit's top activating dataset examples, the most direct V6 condition. Accuracy is 66–67%, only ~6 points over no references and indistinguishable from simple heuristics. The per-condition mapping is unstated in the text (Fig. 3A bars give Natural 0.66±0.03, Mixed ~0.67, Blur ~0.67).

source_check.locator_found: Sec 4.1 (66±3% to 67±5% for other visualization types)
source_check.problem: Range is given for the non-synthetic types together; per-type split is only in the figure, which is garbled.

rows.subject: Center Baseline
rows.operation_detail: Choose the query image with the more eccentric occlusion.
rows.note: A simple positional heuristic, not a visualization-based explanation.
rows.check: Heuristic comparator (Center Baseline), not a measure of explanation fidelity.

rows.subject: Primary Object Baseline
rows.operation_detail: Choose the image whose occlusion hides less information from the most prominent object.
rows.uncertainty: ±1%; the text describes an estimated expectation and standard deviation
rows.note: The estimate uses randomized choices for trials without a clear primary object.
rows.check: Heuristic comparator (Primary Object Baseline). The majority-vote variant reaches 0.70±0.02 (Appx A.1.3).

rows.subject: Variance Baseline
rows.operation_detail: Choose the image whose occluded pixels have lower standard deviation.
rows.note: A simple image-statistic heuristic, not a visualization-based explanation.

rows.subject: Saliency Baseline
rows.operation_detail: Choose the image whose occlusion covers a lower-saliency region, using DeepGaze IIE.
rows.note: The reported accuracy is slightly below chance.
rows.check: Heuristic comparator (Saliency Baseline); its accuracy is at chance.

relationships.condition: InceptionV1 units; occlusion-intervention task; natural, synthetic, mixed or blurred activating references
relationships.reason: With top activating references, humans predict occlusion effects at 66–67%, only ~6 points above no references (60%) and near heuristics (63%) (R1, R3 vs R2).
relationships.display_finding: With top activating references, humans predicted occlusion effects at 66–67%, only about 6 points above having no references (60%) and close to simple heuristics (63%).

source_check.notes: The abstract gives 68±4% (synthetic) and 66±3% to 67±3% (others), but Sec 4.1 gives 67±4% and 66±3% to 67±5%. The rows and statements use Sec 4.1. The 63% is for the two best heuristics (Object 63±1%, Variance 63%). The A.3 replication used MTurk, the 3x3 branch only and 130 participants per condition.

reader_labels.label: limits_scope
reader_labels.condition: Synthetic references compared with no references and the other visualization conditions
reader_labels.reason: Accuracy with synthetic references is 67 ± 4%, while no references gives 60 ± 3%; the study reports no significant synthetic advantage over alternative visualizations, so the measured human predictive benefit is limited rather than a direct test of an explanation's own firing predictions (R1–R3).
